Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,
\]

so that

\[
m^2\le n < (m+1)^2.
\]

We will first derive necessary conditions on any prime divisor of \(n\).

---

### 1. Prime divisors of \(n\)

Let \(p^a\parallel n\), meaning \(p^a\mid n\) but \(p^{a+1}\nmid n\).

#### Case A: \(p\le m\)

Then \(p\mid m!\). Hence

\[
v_p\bigl((m!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!\,v_p(m!)\ge n!.
\]

Since \(a\le n\le n!\), we have \(p^a\mid (m!)^{n!}\).  
Because \(n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450\), reducing modulo \(p^a\) gives

\[
450\equiv 0 \pmod{p^a}.
\]

Thus

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

So every prime power of \(n\) coming from primes \(\le m\) must divide \(450\).

#### Case B: \(p>m\)

Then \(p^2>n\), so \(a=1\). Also \(p\nmid m!\).

Since \(p\mid n\), we have \(n\ge p\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Since \(p\mid n\) and \(n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450\),

\[
1+450\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Therefore any prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be either \(11\) or \(41\).

---

### 2. Bounding possible \(n\)

We now bound any solution \(n\).

#### If \(m\le 34\)

Then

\[
n<35^2=1225,
\]

so

\[
n\le 1224<1230.
\]

#### If \(35\le m\le 40\)

Any prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be \(41\). Let \(S\) be the part of \(n\) consisting of prime powers whose primes are \(\le m\). From Case A,

\[
S\mid 450.
\]

If \(41\nmid n\), then \(n=S\le 450\).

If \(41\mid n\), then since \(41>m\) and \(41^2>n\),

\[
n=41S.
\]

Also \(m\le 40\) gives \(n<41^2\), so \(S<41\). Since \(S\mid 450\), the largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\). Therefore

\[
n=41S\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

#### If \(m\ge 41\)

No prime divisor of \(n\) can be larger than \(m\), because any such prime would have to be \(11\) or \(41\), both of which are \(\le m\). Thus all prime factors of \(n\) are \(\le m\), so by Case A every prime power in \(n\) divides \(450\). Hence

\[
n\mid 450,
\]

so

\[
n\le 450<1230.
\]

Thus every solution satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 3. Verify that \(n=1230\) works

For \(n=1230\),

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor =35,
\]

since

\[
35^2=1225\le 1230<1296=36^2.
\]

Also

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

We check divisibility by each prime factor.

- Modulo \(2,3,5\):  
  \(35!\) is divisible by \(2,3,5\), so \((35!)^{1230!}\equiv 0\pmod{2,3,5}\). Also \(450\equiv 0\pmod{2,3,5}\). Hence the sum is divisible by \(2,3,5\).

- Modulo \(41\):  
  Since \(35!\not\equiv 0\pmod{41}\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat gives

  \[
  (35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
  \]

  Also

  \[
  450\equiv -1\pmod{41},
  \]

  so

  \[
  (35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
  \]

Thus \(1230\) divides

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Therefore the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
